items.title: The Adornment of Discourse Opens: Mastering Both Positions, Perfecting Speech

items.zh: 論莊嚴者，略有五種。一、善自他宗，二、言具圓滿，三、無畏，四、敦肅，五、應供。
items.en: The adornment of discourse: briefly, it has five kinds. First, mastery of one's own and other positions; second, speech perfected in every respect; third, fearlessness; fourth, dignified restraint; and fifth, being worthy of respect.

items.zh: 善自他宗者，謂如有一，若於此法毘奈耶中深生愛樂，即於此論宗旨，讀誦、受持、聽聞、思惟、純熟修行，已善、已說、已明。若於彼法毘奈耶中不愛不樂，然於彼論宗旨，讀誦、受持、聞思純熟，而不修行，然已善、已說、已明。是名善自他宗。
items.en: Mastery of one's own and other positions: it means that one who deeply delights in this Dharma and discipline reads, recites, upholds, hears, reflects on, and ripens in practising its own thesis, until it is thoroughly mastered, thoroughly articulable, and thoroughly clear. And though taking no delight in another's dharma and discipline, one still reads, recites, upholds, hears, and reflects on that thesis until thoroughly ripened — without practising it — so that it too is thoroughly mastered, thoroughly articulable, and thoroughly clear. This is called mastery of one's own and other positions.

items.zh: 言具圓滿者，謂如有一，凡有所說，皆以其聲，不以非聲。何等為聲？謂具五德，乃名為聲。一、不鄙陋，二、輕易，三、雄朗，四、相應，五、義善。
items.en: Speech perfected in every respect: it means that whatever one says, one always speaks with genuine speech, never with what falls short of it. What is genuine speech? Only speech possessing five virtues deserves the name: first, free of rustic, provincial diction; second, readily understood; third, vigorous and clear; fourth, coherent; and fifth, wholesome in meaning.

items.zh: 不鄙陋者，謂離邊方邊國鄙俚言詞。輕易者，謂有所說，皆以世間共用言詞。雄朗者，所謂依義建立言詞，能成彼義巧妙雄壯。相應者，謂前後法義相符不散。義善者，謂能引發勝生、定勝、無有顛倒。又此聲論，由九種相言具圓滿。一、不雜亂，二、不麁獷，三、辯了，四、限量，五、與義相應，六、以時，七、決定，八、顯了，九、相續。如是一切相，總名言具圓滿。
items.en: 'Not provincial' means free from the crude diction of border regions and outlying countries. 'Readily understood' means that whatever is said uses words commonly used in the world. 'Vigorous and clear' means words established on the basis of meaning, which can convey that meaning skilfully and forcefully. 'Coherent' means that the dharmas and meanings agree from beginning to end and do not scatter. 'Wholesome in meaning' means able to lead to a higher birth and the highest good, without distortion. Further, this speech is complete in its use of words through nine features: first, not confused; second, not coarse; third, articulate; fourth, measured; fifth, connected with the meaning; sixth, timely; seventh, decisive; eighth, clear; ninth, continuous. All these features together are called completeness in the use of words.

items.title: The Adornment of Discourse Completes: Fearlessness, Dignity, and Twenty-Seven Praised Virtues

items.zh: 無畏者：謂如有一、處在多眾雜眾大眾執眾諦眾善眾等中、其心無有下劣恒懼，身無戰汗，面無怖色，音無謇吃，語無怯弱。如是說者、名為無畏。敦肅者：謂如有一、待時方說而不嚵速；是名敦肅。
items.en: Fearlessness: it means that, standing before a large assembly, a mixed assembly, a royal assembly, a judging assembly, a wise assembly, or an assembly skilled [in the Dharma], one's mind is free of inferior anxiety, one's body does not tremble or sweat, one's face shows no fear, one's voice does not stammer, and one's speech shows no timidity. Speaking in this way is called fearlessness. Dignified restraint: it means waiting for the right moment to speak, never cutting in before the other has finished. This is called dignified restraint.

items.zh: 應供者：謂如有一，為性調善，不惱於他；終不違越諸調善者調善之地；隨順他心而起言說；以時，如實，能引義利；言詞柔軟，如對善友。是名應供。
items.en: Worthy of respect: it means that one is, by nature, well-tamed and gentle, never troubling others; never overstepping the bounds with those who are well-tamed; speaking in accord with another's state of mind; speaking at the right time, truthfully, and in a way that brings real benefit; and speaking with words so gentle it is as though addressing a cherished friend. This is called being worthy of respect.

items.zh: 若有依此五論莊嚴興言論者，當知復有二十七種稱讚功德。何等名為二十七種？一、眾所敬重；二、言必信受；三、處大眾中都無所畏；四、於他宗旨深知過隙；五、於自宗旨知殊勝德；六、無有僻執，於所受論情無偏黨；七、於自正法及毘奈耶無能引奪；八、於他所說速能了悟；九、於他所說速能領受；十、於他所說速能酬對；十一、具語言德，令眾愛樂；十二、悅可信解此明論者；十三、能善宣釋義句文字；十四、令身無倦；十五、令心無倦；十六、言不謇澁；十七、辯才無盡；十八、身不頓顇；十九、念無忘失；二十、心無損惱；二十一、咽喉無損；二十二、凡所宣吐分明易了；二十三、善護自心，令無忿怒；二十四、善順他心，令無憤恚；二十五、令對論者心生淨信；二十六、凡有所行不招怨對；二十七、廣大名稱，聲流十方，世咸傳唱此大法師，處大師數。
items.en: One who takes up discourse resting on these five adornments should be known to gain, in addition, twenty-seven praised virtues: first, being honoured by all; second, one's word being trusted and accepted without question; third, complete fearlessness before any assembly... seventeenth, inexhaustible eloquence... twenty-fifth, inspiring genuine faith in one's opponent; twenty-sixth, that whatever one does draws no enmity; and twenty-seventh, a reputation so vast it spreads in every direction, until the world speaks of this person as a great master, counted among the ranks of the great teachers.

items.zh: 如受欲者、以末尼、真珠、琉璃等寶，廁環釧等寶莊嚴具以自莊嚴，威德熾盛，光明普照。如是論者，以二十七稱讚功德，廁此五種論莊嚴具，以自莊嚴，威德熾盛，光明普照。是故名此為論莊嚴。
items.en: It is like one who enjoys sensual pleasures, adorning themselves with maṇi jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, and the like, set among bracelets and rings, so that their splendour blazes forth and their radiance shines everywhere. Just so, one engaged in discourse, adorning themselves with these twenty-seven praised virtues set among these five adornments of discourse, has splendour that blazes forth and radiance that shines everywhere. This is why this is called the adornment of discourse.
This is called the adornment of discourse.

items.title: Discourse's Defeat Opens: Thirteen Ways to Formally Concede

items.zh: 論墮負者，謂有三種。一、捨言，二、言屈，三、言過。捨言者，謂立論者，以十三種詞謝對論者，捨所言論。
items.en: Discourse's defeat: it has three kinds. First, formally conceding; second, being verbally cornered; and third, speech itself carrying a fault. Formally conceding: it means that the one positing the thesis addresses the opponent with thirteen kinds of words, thereby abandoning the discourse advanced.
What are the thirteen kinds of words?

items.zh: 謂立論者謝對論者曰：我論不善，汝論為善；我不善觀，汝為善觀；我論無理，汝論有理；我論無能，汝論有能；我論屈伏，汝論成立；我之辯才唯極於此，過此已上更善思量，當為汝說；且置是事，我不復言。
items.en: The one positing the thesis addresses the opponent, saying: my discourse is unskillful, yours is skilful; I did not observe well, you observed well; my discourse has no principle, yours has principle; my discourse has no capacity, yours has capacity; my discourse is overcome, yours stands established; my eloquence reaches only this far — beyond this, I would need to reflect further before I could speak to you; let this matter rest — I will say no more.

items.zh: 以如是等十三種詞謝對論者，捨所言論。捨所論故，當知被破，為他所勝，墮在他後，屈伏於彼。是故捨言，名墮負處。
items.en: Addressing the opponent with these thirteen kinds of words, one abandons the discourse advanced. Having abandoned it, know that one is thereby refuted, overcome by the other, fallen behind, and subdued by them. This is why formally conceding is called falling into defeat.

blocks.text: Today the treatise describes the qualities of a good debater, the "adornments of discourse", and then begins the ways a debater loses. The adornments read like a portrait of a good teacher: knowledgeable, well spoken, unafraid, courteous, and fair.

The first adornment is mastery of one's own and others' positions. Venerable Miào Jìng adds a traditional caution: Buddhists may study other teachings, but "must regard them as poison; only the Dharma is nectar." A modern reader may put it more gently: study other views thoroughly, but know which one you are practising.
The second is perfect speech. Its first virtue is 不鄙陋: not "provincial". Venerable Miào Jìng: someone who has read little and "speaks in a rustic way". Then clarity, gentleness, relevance, and more.

**Fearlessness**: the *Pīxún jì* divides its marks into mental (no anxiety), bodily (no trembling, no fearful face), and verbal (no stammering). **Restraint** (敦肅): waiting for the right moment, not interrupting. Venerable Miào Jìng: "When the other's passage isn't finished and you speak in the middle, that is 儳." Ru-Yi's "blurting out" misses this; the virtue is letting the other finish. **Worthiness**: "never transgressing the tamed ground of the well-tamed": Venerable Miào Jìng: if the opponent is gentle, one does not attack him harshly.

A debater with these adornments earns twenty-seven praised qualities, such as being honoured, trusted, and invited. Master Cháng Bǎi: they never go beyond the five adornments. Ru-Yi's rendering of two gems in this passage is questionable: 末尼 is the *maṇi* jewel, 琉璃 is usually beryl.

Defeat in debate is shown in three ways: abandoning one's speech, being cornered, and faults of speech. Thirteen ways of formally conceding include "Let this matter rest; I will say no more." Master Cháng Bǎi relays a story told by Venerable Miào Jìng: before his death, the Buddhist scholar Ouyang Jingwu told his students that he had lost an argument and that the matter should not be raised again. An honest concession is itself a virtue.

A whole science of debate may seem far from meditation. But Indian Buddhism lived among rival schools, and its teachers had to defend the Dharma in public. The rules the treatise gives are, at heart, rules of honest and respectful speech: know the subject, speak clearly, let others finish, do not bully the gentle, and admit when you are wrong.

quiz.q: Mastering other positions means studying them. What attitude does Venerable Miào Jìng prescribe when Buddhists study worldly teachings?
options: regard them as poison — worldly teachings are poisonous; only the Dharma is nectar
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: Buddhists may study worldly teachings, but must regard them as poison — only the Dharma is nectar. The treatise: one masters other positions without practising them. Master Cháng Bǎi: mastery reveals their faults.

quiz.q: The first virtue of speech, 不鄙陋, is rendered "free of coarseness" — the same word used for 麤獷 in §30. How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain it?
options: not provincial — little reading, no bookish air, speech that sounds rustic; the text means avoiding backwater idioms
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Someone who has read little, without a scholarly air, speaks in a rustic way — that's the meaning." The omitted text: free of the idioms of remote borderlands. "Coarseness" collides with §30.

quiz.q: How does the Pixunji divide the marks of fearlessness — mind, body, face, voice, words?
options: the fearless mind is mental expression; no trembling or fearful face, bodily; no stammer or timid words, verbal
quiz.why: The *Pixunji*: a mind free of anxiety is mental expression; a body that doesn't tremble and a face without fear, bodily; a voice that doesn't stammer and words without timidity, verbal. Venerable Miào Jìng recounts overcoming stage fright.

quiz.q: Restraint is "waiting for the moment, not 儳速." How does Venerable Miào Jìng define 儳, and how does the English fare?
options: cutting in before the other has finished — the English "blurting out" misses "not interrupting"
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "When the other's passage isn't finished and you speak in the middle, that is 儳." Master Cháng Bǎi: speak the right words at the right time, without interjecting. The English misses the interruption.

quiz.q: Worthiness: "never transgressing the tamed ground of the well-tamed." The English reads it as the speaker staying in bounds. How does Venerable Miào Jìng read it?
options: "the well-tamed" are the other party — if the opponent is gentle, one does not assail him; the "ground" is the mind
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: if the other party is gentle and good-natured, one will not assail him; "the ground of the tamed" is the mind. Master Cháng Bǎi links worthiness to the five virtues required for raising faults.

quiz.q: For the concession "let this matter rest — I will say no more," whose example does Master Cháng Bǎi cite?
options: Venerable Miào Jìng's example of Ouyang Jingwu, who before dying told his students he had lost and the matter should be dropped
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: it is said that before his death Ouyang Jingwu told his disciples, "I lost to him; don't speak of this topic again" — explicitly crediting the example to Venerable Miào Jìng. The note misattributes it.
